# Hierarchical Queries

Walking a tree that is stored in a single self-referencing column. One row per node, one column
pointing at the parent's key, and a query that traverses it to arbitrary depth without knowing the
depth in advance. Oracle spells this `CONNECT BY`; ANSI SQL spells it as a recursive CTE.

## The one thing that is easy to get backwards

Direction lives entirely in which side of the join predicate carries `PRIOR`, and the source file
states it at the top rather than leaving it to be discovered per query:

```
CONNECT BY PRIOR nickname = chief   walks DOWN  (root -> subordinates)
CONNECT BY PRIOR chief = nickname   walks UP    (leaf -> chain of chiefs)
```

Both appear in [[oracle-database-laboratories]] against the same `CATS.chief` self-reference — see
[[circular-foreign-key]] for why a self-reference is *not* the awkward case.

## The pseudocolumns

| Construct | What it gives |
|---|---|
| `LEVEL` | depth **relative to `START WITH`**, not to the top of the tree — 1 at whatever the start clause selected |
| `SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(col, sep)` | the whole root-to-node path as one delimited string |
| `CONNECT_BY_ROOT col` | the value of `col` at the row the walk started from |

`LEVEL` is also how the tree gets *drawn*: `LPAD(' ', (LEVEL-1)*4) || …` renders the indentation, one
of the cheapest ways to make a relational structure legible — the same instinct as
[[make-the-formal-object-observable]] reached without any tooling.

## `WHERE` is applied after the walk

The subtlety worth naming: filtering does not prune the subtree.

> "The WHERE clause is applied after the tree is walked, so pruning a cat here does not prune its
> subordinates -- which is exactly what is wanted: the shape of the hierarchy is preserved and only
> the display is filtered."
> — Oracle-Database-Laboratories/sql/02_queries/02_hierarchical_queries.sql, 2026-07-25

To prune the traversal itself you add the predicate to `CONNECT BY`, not to `WHERE`. Two clauses, two
different meanings, and the difference is invisible on data whose filtered nodes happen to be leaves.

## The same answer three ways

"The chain of chiefs above every rank-and-file cat" is written three times in one file, and the
comparison is the exercise — see [[multiple-solutions-side-by-side]]:

| Formulation | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Repeated `LEFT JOIN`**, one per level | explicit and portable, but **hard-codes the depth**: a fourth tier needs another join |
| **`CONNECT BY` + `PIVOT`** | adapts to any depth by adding a value to the `PIVOT` `IN` list; still one column per level |
| **`CONNECT BY` + `SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH`** | depth-independent, but the answer is one string, so downstream consumers must parse it |

There is no winner. The trade is *columns you can join against* versus *a shape that survives a deeper
tree*, and picking one is a statement about what happens to the result next.

## The same walk over pointers

`04_object_relational/03_ref_navigation.sql` runs `CONNECT BY PRIOR c.nickname = c.chief.nickname`
over a `REF` column instead of a value-carrying foreign key. The traversal is unchanged; only the
dereference differs — see [[object-relational-model]].
